name: Chapter 14: Probability
description: Events and their algebra, axiomatic probability, addition rule, complement, equally likely outcomes, plus conditional probability and independence for exams.

cards.term: Define an event.
cards.definition: Any subset of the sample space S of a random experiment

cards.term: When does an event E occur?
cards.definition: When the outcome ω of the experiment satisfies ω ∈ E; if ω ∉ E the event has not occurred

cards.term: Two coins are tossed: sample space and the event “exactly one head”.
cards.definition: S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}; E = {HT, TH}

cards.term: Impossible event and sure event?
cards.definition: Impossible: the empty set φ (e.g. a multiple of 7 on a die). Sure: the whole sample space S (e.g. “odd or even”)

cards.term: Simple (elementary) event and compound event?
cards.definition: Simple: exactly one sample point, e.g. {HH}. Compound: more than one sample point, e.g. “exactly one head in three tosses” = {HTT, THT, TTH}. A sample space with n points has n simple events

cards.term: Tree diagram for three coins
cards.definition: Three coins: 8 equally likely outcomes; P(exactly 2 heads)=3/8, P(at least 2 heads)=1/2, P(3 heads)=1/8

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Three coins · tree of outcomes

Three coins are tossed. List the sample space with a tree and find P(exactly two heads) and P(at least two heads).

Branch H/T at each toss.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Three coins · tree of outcomes

Three coins are tossed. List the sample space with a tree and find P(exactly two heads) and P(at least two heads).

2 × 2 × 2 = 8 equally likely outcomes. Exactly two heads: HHT, HTH, THH → 3/8. At least two heads: those three plus HHH → 4/8 = 1/2.

cards.term: Two-dice sample space of 36 outcomes
cards.definition: Two dice: 36 equally likely ordered pairs; P(sum 7) = 6/36 = 1/6, the most likely; P(sum ≥ 10) = 6/36; (1,6) and (6,1) are different

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Sample space of two dice

Two dice are rolled. How many equally likely outcomes are there? Shade the events “sum = 7” and “sum ≥ 10”.

Order matters: the dice are distinguishable.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Sample space of two dice

Two dice are rolled. How many equally likely outcomes are there? Shade the events “sum = 7” and “sum ≥ 10”.

36 ordered pairs (first die, second die), all equally likely: n(S) = 36.

Sum 7: (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1) → 6/36 = 1/6 (the most likely sum). Sum ≥ 10: (4,6), (5,5), (5,6), (6,4), (6,5), (6,6) → 6/36 = 1/6.

Trap: (1,6) and (6,1) are different outcomes.

cards.term: Complementary event A′ (“not A”)?
cards.definition: A′ = S − A = {ω ∈ S : ω ∉ A}. P(A′) = 1 − P(A)

cards.term: Events “A or B”, “A and B”, “A but not B” as sets?
cards.definition: A ∪ B, A ∩ B, A − B = A ∩ B′

cards.term: Example 1: die; A = prime = {2, 3, 5}, B = odd = {1, 3, 5}. Find A or B, A and B, A but not B, not A.
cards.definition: {1, 2, 3, 5}; {3, 5}; {2}; {1, 4, 6}

cards.term: Two dice: A = first throw is 6, B = sum ≥ 11. Find A ∩ B.
Mutually exclusive events: definition?
cards.definition: A ∩ B = φ: they cannot occur together. Simple events of a sample space are always mutually exclusive

cards.term: Die: A = odd, B = less than 4. Mutually exclusive?
cards.definition: No: A = {1, 3, 5}, B = {1, 2, 3} share 1 and 3

cards.term: Exhaustive events?
cards.definition: E₁ ∪ E₂ ∪ … ∪ Eₙ = S: at least one of them must occur. If also pairwise disjoint they are mutually exclusive and exhaustive (a partition of S)

cards.term: Example 2: two dice, A sum even, B sum multiple of 3, C sum < 4, D sum > 11. Which pairs are mutually exclusive?
cards.definition: C = {(1,1), (2,1), (1,2)} and D = {(6,6)} share nothing: only (C, D). All other pairs overlap (e.g. A ∩ B contains (3,3))

cards.term: Example 3: three coins: A no head, B exactly one head, C at least two heads. Exclusive and exhaustive?
cards.definition: A = {TTT}, B has 3 outcomes, C has 4: pairwise disjoint and A ∪ B ∪ C = S → yes, both

cards.term: Ex 14.1 Q1: die; E = “shows 4”, F = “shows an even number”. Mutually exclusive?
cards.definition: No: E = {4} ⊂ F = {2, 4, 6}, so 4 is common

cards.term: Ex 14.1 Q2: die events A: < 7, B: > 7, C: multiple of 3, D: < 4, E: even > 4, F: not < 3.
Ex 14.1 Q2: A ∪ B, A ∩ B, B ∪ C, E ∩ F, D ∩ E, A − C, D − E, E ∩ F′, F′.
Ex 14.1 Q3: two dice, A sum > 8, B a 2 on either die, C sum ≥ 7 and a multiple of 3. Exclusive pairs?
cards.definition: A has 10 outcomes, B has 11, C = {(3,6), (4,5), (5,4), (6,3), (6,6)}. A and B cannot meet (max sum with a 2 is 8); B and C cannot meet. So (A, B) and (B, C) are mutually exclusive; A and C are not

cards.term: Ex 14.1 Q4: three coins; A = 3 heads, B = 2 heads and a tail, C = 3 tails, D = head on the first coin.
cards.definition: Mutually exclusive: A,B; A,C; B,C; C,D. Simple: A and C. Compound: B and D

cards.term: Ex 14.1 Q5: examples of events for three coins.
cards.definition: Two exclusive: “3 heads” and “3 tails”. Three exclusive and exhaustive: “no head”, “exactly 1–2 heads”, “3 heads”. Not exclusive: “first is H” and “last is H”. Exclusive not exhaustive: “3 heads”, “3 tails”

cards.term: Method: showing events are mutually exclusive / exhaustive.
cards.definition: Write the events as sets. Exclusive: check each pair has empty intersection. Exhaustive: check the union is S (counts add to n(S) if also disjoint)

cards.term: Axioms of probability?
cards.definition: (i) P(E) ≥ 0; (ii) P(S) = 1; (iii) P(E ∪ F) = P(E) + P(F) for mutually exclusive E, F

cards.term: Prove P(φ) = 0 from the axioms.
cards.definition: E and φ are disjoint: P(E) = P(E ∪ φ) = P(E) + P(φ) → P(φ) = 0

cards.term: Probability on a finite sample space {ω₁, …, ωₙ}?
cards.definition: Assign P(ωᵢ) with 0 ≤ P(ωᵢ) ≤ 1 and ΣP(ωᵢ) = 1. Then P(A) = Σ P(ωᵢ) over ωᵢ ∈ A

cards.term: A coin: P(H) = ½ = P(T). Are P(H) = ¼, P(T) = ¾ also valid?
cards.definition: Yes. Any p and 1 − p with 0 ≤ p ≤ 1 satisfy the axioms: infinitely many valid assignments. Equal probabilities are just one choice (the fair coin)

cards.term: Example 4: which assignments to six outcomes are valid: (a) six positive probabilities summing to 1, (b) 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, (c) with two negative values, (d) with 3/2, (e) 0.1, 0.2, …, 0.6?
cards.definition: (a) valid (b) valid (c) no: negative probabilities (d) no: 3/2 > 1 (e) no: sum = 2.1

cards.term: Validity test for a proposed assignment?
cards.definition: Check (1) every value in [0, 1] and (2) the values sum to exactly 1. Fail either and it is invalid

cards.term: Ex 14.2 Q1: which of the seven-outcome assignments are invalid: (c) 0.1, 0.2, …, 0.7; (d) −0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, −0.2, 0.1, 0.3?
cards.definition: (c) sums to 2.8 → invalid. (d) has negative values → invalid. (a) 0.1, 0.01, 0.05, 0.03, 0.01, 0.2, 0.6 sums to 1.0 → valid

cards.term: Equally likely outcomes: probability of an event?
cards.definition: \(P(E) = \dfrac{n(E)}{n(S)} = \dfrac{m}{n}\) (m favourable outcomes out of n equally likely outcomes)

cards.term: Why is P(each outcome) = 1/n for n equally likely outcomes?
cards.definition: The n probabilities are equal (p each) and sum to 1: np = 1 → p = 1/n

cards.term: Addition rule for any two events?
cards.definition: \(P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)\). If mutually exclusive, the last term is 0

cards.term: Why do we subtract P(A ∩ B)?
cards.definition: Outcomes in A ∩ B are counted twice in P(A) + P(B). Example (3 coins): A = {HHT, HTH, THH}, B = {HTH, THH, HHH}: 3/8 + 3/8 = 6/8 but P(A ∪ B) = 4/8

cards.term: Proof of the addition rule (short)?
cards.definition: A ∪ B = A ∪ (B − A) (disjoint) and B = (A ∩ B) ∪ (B − A) (disjoint). Subtract: P(A ∪ B) − P(B) = P(A) − P(A ∩ B)

cards.term: Probability of “not A”?
cards.definition: P(A′) = 1 − P(A) since A and A′ are mutually exclusive and exhaustive: P(A) + P(A′) = 1

cards.term: Complement trick: P(at least one) = ?
cards.definition: 1 − P(none). E.g. at least one tail in two tosses = 1 − P(HH) = 3/4

cards.term: Inclusion–exclusion for three events (Example 11)?
cards.definition: \(P(A\cup B\cup C) = \sum P(A) - \sum P(A\cap B) + P(A\cap B\cap C)\)

cards.term: Venn diagram probabilities for two events
cards.definition: P(E)=0.05, P(F)=0.10, P(E∩F)=0.02: E only 0.03, F only 0.08, neither 0.87, not both 0.98, exactly one 0.11

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 7 · Venn probabilities

P(E) = 0.05, P(F) = 0.10, P(E ∩ F) = 0.02. Fill each region. Find P(neither), P(not both) and P(exactly one).

Subtract the overlap from each event.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 7 · Venn probabilities

P(E) = 0.05, P(F) = 0.10, P(E ∩ F) = 0.02. Fill each region. Find P(neither), P(not both) and P(exactly one).

E only = 0.05 − 0.02 = 0.03; F only = 0.10 − 0.02 = 0.08. P(E ∪ F) = 0.13 → P(neither) = 0.87.

P(not both) = 1 − 0.02 = 0.98. P(exactly one) = 0.03 + 0.08 = 0.11. Regions of the Venn diagram add to 1.

cards.term: Example 5: one card from 52. P(diamond), P(not an ace), P(black), P(not a diamond), P(not black)?
cards.definition: 1/4; 12/13; 1/2; 3/4; 1/2

cards.term: Example 6: bag with 4 red, 3 blue, 2 yellow discs. P(red), P(yellow), P(blue), P(not blue), P(red or blue)?
cards.definition: 4/9, 2/9, 1/3, 2/3, 7/9 (red and blue are exclusive, so add)

cards.term: Example 7: P(E) = 0.05, P(F) = 0.10, P(E ∩ F) = 0.02. Find P(neither), P(at least one fails), P(only one qualifies).
cards.definition: P(E ∪ F) = 0.13 → 0.87; 1 − 0.02 = 0.98; 0.03 + 0.08 = 0.11

cards.term: Example 8: committee of 2 chosen from 2 men and 2 women. P(no man), P(one man), P(two men)?
cards.definition: Total ⁴C₂ = 6: 1/6, 4/6 = 2/3, 1/6

cards.term: Ex 14.2 Q2: a coin is tossed twice. P(at least one tail)?
cards.definition: 3/4
1/2, 2/3, 1/6, 0, 5/6

cards.term: Ex 14.2 Q4: a card from 52: number of sample points; P(ace of spades); P(ace); P(black).
cards.definition: 52; 1/52; 1/13; 1/2

cards.term: Ex 14.2 Q5: a coin marked 1 and 6 and a die are tossed. P(sum = 3) and P(sum = 12).
cards.definition: Sum 3 needs (1, 2); sum 12 needs (6, 6): each 1/12 (12 equally likely outcomes)

cards.term: Ex 14.2 Q6: 4 men and 6 women on a council; one member is picked at random. P(woman)?
cards.definition: 6/10 = 3/5

cards.term: Ex 14.2 Q7: four tosses; win ₹1 per head, lose ₹1.50 per tail. Possible amounts and their probabilities?
cards.definition: k heads → 2.5k − 6: −6 (1/16), −3.5 (1/4), −1 (3/8), +1.5 (1/4), +4 (1/16): five different amounts

cards.term: Ex 14.2 Q8: three coins. P(3 heads), P(2 heads), P(at least 2), P(at most 2), P(no head), P(3 tails), P(exactly two tails), P(no tail), P(at most two tails).
Ex 14.2 Q9: P(A) = 2/11. Find P(not A).
cards.definition: 9/11

cards.term: Ex 14.2 Q10: a letter chosen at random from ASSASSINATION. P(vowel), P(consonant).
cards.definition: 13 letters, vowels A, A, I, A, I, O = 6: 6/13 and 7/13

cards.term: Ex 14.2 Q11: lottery: choose 6 numbers from 1–20; probability of matching the fixed six?
cards.definition: 1/²⁰C₆ = 1/38760 (order does not matter)

cards.term: Ex 14.2 Q12: are these consistent? (i) P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.7, P(A ∩ B) = 0.6; (ii) P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4, P(A ∪ B) = 0.8.
cards.definition: (i) No: P(A ∩ B) cannot exceed P(A). (ii) P(A ∩ B) = 0.9 − 0.8 = 0.1 ≤ min → consistent
P(B) = 0.6 − 0.35 + 0.25 = 0.5; P(A ∩ B) = 0.85 − 0.7 = 0.15

cards.term: Ex 14.2 Q14: P(A) = 3/5, P(B) = 1/5, mutually exclusive. P(A or B)?
cards.definition: 4/5

cards.term: Ex 14.2 Q15: P(E) = 1/4, P(F) = 1/2, P(E and F) = 1/8. Find P(E or F) and P(not E and not F).
cards.definition: 5/8 and 3/8

cards.term: Ex 14.2 Q16: P(not E or not F) = 0.25. Are E and F mutually exclusive?
cards.definition: P(E ∩ F) = 1 − 0.25 = 0.75 ≠ 0 → not mutually exclusive

cards.term: Ex 14.2 Q17: P(A) = 0.42, P(B) = 0.48, P(A and B) = 0.16. Find P(not A), P(not B), P(A or B).
cards.definition: 0.58, 0.52, 0.74

cards.term: Ex 14.2 Q18: 40% study Maths, 30% Biology, 10% both. P(Maths or Biology)?
cards.definition: 0.4 + 0.3 − 0.1 = 0.6

cards.term: Ex 14.2 Q19: P(pass first) = 0.8, P(pass second) = 0.7, P(at least one) = 0.95. P(both)?
Ex 14.2 Q20: P(pass English and Hindi) = 0.5, P(neither) = 0.1, P(English) = 0.75. P(Hindi)?
Ex 14.2 Q21: 60 students; 30 NCC, 32 NSS, 24 both. P(NCC or NSS), P(neither), P(NSS but not NCC).
cards.definition: Union = 38: 38/60 = 19/30; 22/60 = 11/30; 8/60 = 2/15

cards.term: Example 9: four cities visited in random order (24 orders). P(A before B)? P(A before B before C)?
cards.definition: 12/24 = 1/2; 4/24 = 1/6 (by symmetry: 1/3! for any fixed order of three named cities)

cards.term: Example 9 (iii)–(v): P(A first and B last); P(A first or second); P(A just before B).
cards.definition: 2/24 = 1/12; 12/24 = 1/2; 6/24 = 1/4 (treat AB as a block: 3! = 6)

cards.term: Example 10: a 7-card hand from 52. P(all four kings), P(exactly 3 kings), P(at least 3 kings)?
cards.definition: 1/7735; 9/1547 (⁴C₃·⁴⁸C₄/⁵²C₇); 46/7735

cards.term: Example 12: five teams in a relay; P(A, B, C finish 1st, 2nd, 3rd in that order); P(they are the first three in any order)?
cards.definition: Sample space ⁵P₃ = 60: 1/60; 3! orders: 6/60 = 1/10

cards.term: Misc Q1: box of 10 red, 20 blue, 30 green marbles; 5 drawn. P(all blue), P(at least one green)?
cards.definition: ²⁰C₅/⁶⁰C₅ = 34/11977 ≈ 0.0028; 1 − ³⁰C₅/⁶⁰C₅ = 4367/4484 ≈ 0.974

cards.term: Misc Q2: 4 cards from 52. P(3 diamonds and 1 spade)?
cards.definition: ¹³C₃ · ¹³C₁ / ⁵²C₄ = 286 × 13/270725 = 286/20825 ≈ 0.0137

cards.term: Misc Q3: a die with two faces marked 1, three faces 2, one face 3. P(2), P(1 or 3), P(not 3).
cards.definition: 3/6 = 1/2; 3/6 = 1/2; 5/6

cards.term: Misc Q4: 10000 tickets, 10 prizes. P(no prize) with one ticket; two tickets.
Misc Q5: 100 students in sections of 40 and 60. P(you and your friend in the same section)? Different?
cards.definition: You are in the 40-section with probability 0.4 (friend joins: 39/99); in the 60-section 0.6 (59/99): 17/33 and 16/33

cards.term: Misc Q6: three letters put at random into three addressed envelopes. P(at least one letter in its own envelope)?
cards.definition: 1 − P(none) = 1 − 2/6 = 2/3 (2 derangements out of 6)
0.88, 0.12, 0.19, 0.34

cards.term: Misc Q9: 4-digit numbers > 5000 from 0, 1, 3, 5, 7. P(divisible by 5) with repetition; without?
cards.definition: With repetition: 250 numbers, last digit 0 or 5: 100 → 2/5. Without: 48 numbers, 18 end in 0 or 5 → 3/8

cards.term: Misc Q10: a 4-wheel suitcase lock opens with a sequence of four distinct digits. P(guessing it)?
cards.definition: ¹⁰P₄ = 5040 sequences → 1/5040

cards.term: Conditional probability P(A | B)?
cards.definition: \(P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}\), P(B) > 0: the probability of A given that B has occurred (the sample space shrinks to B)

cards.term: Multiplication rule?
cards.definition: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) · P(B | A) = P(B) · P(A | B)

cards.term: Independent events: definition and test?
cards.definition: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) · P(B) (equivalently P(A | B) = P(A)). Independent is not the same as mutually exclusive

cards.term: Trap: mutually exclusive vs independent?
cards.definition: If P(A), P(B) > 0 and A, B are mutually exclusive then P(A ∩ B) = 0 ≠ P(A)P(B): they are dependent. Exclusive events are the most dependent: if one occurs, the other cannot

cards.term: Two dice: P(sum 8 | first die is 3)?
cards.definition: Given a 3, the second must be 5: 1/6

cards.term: Two independent events with P(A) = 0.3, P(B) = 0.4: P(A ∪ B)?
At least one success in n independent trials, each with probability p?
cards.definition: 1 − (1 − p)ⁿ. E.g. at least one six in 3 rolls: 1 − (5/6)³ = 91/216

cards.term: Total probability and Bayes’ theorem (Class 12)?
cards.definition: For a partition E₁, …, Eₙ: P(A) = Σ P(Eᵢ)P(A | Eᵢ); P(Eⱼ | A) = P(Eⱼ)P(A | Eⱼ) / Σ P(Eᵢ)P(A | Eᵢ)

cards.term: Odds in favour and against?
cards.definition: If P(A) = m/(m + n): odds in favour m : n, odds against n : m. P(rain) = 0.2 → odds in favour 1 : 4

cards.term: Card facts to remember?
cards.definition: 52 cards, 4 suits × 13 ranks; 26 red and 26 black; 12 face cards (J, Q, K); 4 aces; 16 honour cards (10, J, Q, K, A) if asked. A hand of n cards: ⁵²Cₙ

cards.term: Number of outcomes for n coins, n dice, and a pair of dice?
cards.definition: 2ⁿ, 6ⁿ, 36

cards.term: Dice sums: which sum is most likely and how many ways for each sum 2 to 12?
cards.definition: 7 (6 ways). Ways: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 for sums 2 through 12

cards.term: Coin sequences: P(exactly k heads in n tosses)?
cards.definition: \(\dfrac{\binom{n}{k}}{2^n}\). E.g. exactly 2 heads in 4 tosses: 6/16 = 3/8

cards.term: Birthday-type problems: P(all n people have different birthdays)?
cards.definition: \(\dfrac{365\cdot364\cdots(365-n+1)}{365^n}\): 1 − this is P(at least two share): for n = 23 it exceeds ½

cards.term:
MCQ: A die is thrown. P(number > 4) is
(a) 1/6 (b) 1/3 (c) 1/2 (d) 2/3
cards.definition: (b) 1/3 (5, 6)

cards.term:
MCQ: Two coins are tossed. P(at least one head) is
(a) 1/4 (b) 1/2 (c) 3/4 (d) 1
cards.definition: (c) 3/4

cards.term:
MCQ: Two dice are thrown. P(sum = 9) is
(a) 1/9 (b) 1/6 (c) 1/12 (d) 5/36

MCQ: A card is drawn from 52. P(king or heart) is
(a) 17/52 (b) 16/52 (c) 4/13 (d) 1/4

cards.definition: 0.4 + 0.5 − 0.2 = (b) 0.7

cards.term:
MCQ: The probability of an event and its complement add to
(a) 0 (b) 1/2 (c) 1 (d) 2
cards.definition: (c) 1

cards.term:
MCQ: A bag has 3 red and 5 blue balls. P(red ball) is
(a) 3/5 (b) 3/8 (c) 5/8 (d) 1/3
cards.definition: (b) 3/8

cards.term:
MCQ: The probability that a leap year has 53 Sundays is
(a) 1/7 (b) 2/7 (c) 3/7 (d) 5/7
cards.definition: 366 = 52 weeks + 2 days; the extra two include Sunday in 2 of 7 cases → (b) 2/7

cards.term: Integer answer (JEE Main): three coins are tossed; if P(at least two heads) = p/q in lowest terms, find p + q.
cards.definition: P = 1/2 → 3

cards.term: Integer answer: two dice are rolled; the number of outcomes with sum 7 or 11 is?
cards.definition: 6 + 2 = 8

cards.term:
Assertion–Reason.
A: P(A ∪ B) ≤ P(A) + P(B).
R: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) and P(A ∩ B) ≥ 0.
(a) Both true, R explains A (b) Both true, R does not (c) A true, R false (d) A false, R true
cards.definition: (a)

cards.term:
Assertion–Reason.
A: If P(A) = 0.6 then P(A′) = 0.4.
R: A and A′ are mutually exclusive and exhaustive.
(a) Both true, R explains A (b) Both true, R does not (c) A true, R false (d) A false, R true
cards.definition: (a)

cards.term: True/False: the probability of an event can be 1.5 if the event is very likely.
cards.definition: False: 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1 always

cards.term: 2-mark: two dice thrown. P(doublet) and P(sum is a prime).
cards.definition: Doublets: 6/36 = 1/6. Prime sums 2, 3, 5, 7, 11: 1 + 2 + 4 + 6 + 2 = 15 → 15/36 = 5/12

cards.term: 3-mark: from a well-shuffled deck, two cards are drawn together. P(both aces)?
cards.definition: ⁴C₂/⁵²C₂ = 6/1326 = 1/221

cards.term: 4-mark: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.3, P(A ∩ B) = 0.1. Find P(A′ ∩ B′) and P(exactly one of A, B).
cards.definition: P(A ∪ B) = 0.7 → 0.3; exactly one: 0.4 + 0.2 = 0.6

cards.term: Case-based: a raffle sells 500 tickets with 3 prizes (a ticket wins at most once). You buy 5. P(win at least one prize)?
cards.definition: 1 − ⁴⁹⁵C₃/⁵⁰⁰C₃ ≈ 0.0298 (about 3%). Rough check: 3 × 5/500 = 0.03
